analysis.investment_thesis: Marc Technocrats is a financially clean micro-cap with zero meaningful debt and consistent earnings, but at ₹48 Cr revenue it is far too small and illiquid for a prudent investor, and the absence of any valuation metrics (P/E, P/B, dividend yield) makes it impossible to ascertain a margin of safety. Without knowing what price Mr. Market is demanding, no rational purchase decision can be made.
key_strengths: Virtually debt-free balance sheet (Total Debt ₹1 Cr vs Equity ₹28 Cr) — the kind of financial conservatism I admire.
Four consecutive years of positive earnings and OCF — meeting my minimum track-record threshold.
Excellent capital efficiency: ROCE of 36.27% suggests the business earns well on what it deploys.
key_risks: No valuation data (P/E, P/B, market cap) provided — I cannot calculate a Graham Number or assess any margin of safety whatsoever.
Dangerously small scale (₹48 Cr revenue, ₹7 Cr net profit) — a single client loss could be catastrophic; Graham preferred established, substantial enterprises.
No dividend history cited — shareholders receive no current return while promoters hold 73.55% of the float, concentrating control and limiting liquidity.
red_flags: SME-exchange listing (YHD-ERR) implies extreme illiquidity and minimal regulatory scrutiny — the intelligent investor avoids such speculative instruments.
Free cash flow (₹3 Cr) materially lags reported net profit (₹7 Cr) in 2025 — earnings quality is questionable when cash generation is less than half of stated profits.

FII ownership of 0.27% signals that institutional analysts have examined and passed — this is not necessarily contrarian opportunity; it may simply reflect legitimate concerns about the company's size and governance.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my vantage point, the first duty of an analyst is to establish what a business is worth and then compare that rigorously to price. I have been given four years of income statements, a balance sheet, and cash flows — but no price, no P/E, no price-to-book. I cannot compute the Graham Number (√22.5 × EPS × BVPS) without market price data. This alone disqualifies the stock from serious consideration under my method. The framework demands I know the price of what I am buying before I buy it.

That said, the underlying business is not without merit. Zero finance costs across all four years, equity growing from ₹14 Cr to ₹28 Cr organically, and ROCE of 36% tell me the consulting operation is genuinely profitable. However, this is a ₹7 Cr net-profit business listed on a thin SME exchange — precisely the terrain where promoter manipulation, accounting opacity, and sudden earnings reversals are endemic. The gap between net profit (₹7 Cr) and free cash flow (₹3 Cr) in 2025 demands explanation before trust is extended. Until I can verify valuation, confirm a dividend policy, and satisfy myself on earnings quality, the intelligent investor's answer is a firm no.
